Whale entangelment

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Once driven to the verge of extinction, southern right whales have made a dramatic comeback and recovery since being given full protection in South African waters, their traditional breeding ground. And it’s not just southern rights – humpback whales, killer whales (Orcas), Brydes and other whale sub-species are increasingly visiting our coast.
But with the increase in numbers, have also come an ever-increasing number of entanglements – whales getting caught in drifting broken pieces of fishing nets and ropes, and in rock lobster and octopus traps. If left entangled, they die a slow and excruciating death. There have been 25 entanglements in the last 2 months- the largest number ever, 15 was high in years gone by. It is now prime whale season in the Western Cape, as the southern right whales arrive from the Southern Ocean and Antarctic for the breeding season.

Enter the South African Whale Disentanglement Network (SAWDN), formed in 2006 to deal with whale entanglements around the African coastline. A volunteer network, it is part of a global initiative to deal with entanglements. Spearheaded by The Department of Environmental Affairs’ Oceans and Coasts division, SAWDN volunteers also include the NSRI, the Police Dive Unit,

But it is a dangerous business. Mature southern right females weigh up to 60 tons, and can reach 80 tons, and their tails and flukes pack a massive punch.
Volunteers get as close as they safely can to the whale and then use razor sharp blades on long poles to cut the ropes piece by piece. Operations can last for several hours, and the whales do not always cooperate. The expensive disentanglement equipment, made in the US and Australia, if often lost or damaged during operations.

The network relies extensively on reports from commercial fishing vessels to find and track down entangled whales, and the companies regularly volunteer their fishing boats and crews to assist SAWDN in disentanglement operations.

Press Release:


Detangling Whales
Once driven to the verge of extinction, Southern Right and other whale species have seen numbers make a dramatic recovery since given full protection in South African waters, their traditional breeding ground. But with the increase in numbers has come ever-increasing entanglements: whales caught in drifting pieces of fishing nets and ropes, rock lobster and octopus traps. If left entangled, they die a slow and excruciating death. Carte Blanche sets out to sea with the highly-trained volunteers doing the dangerous job of disentangling these enormous mammals.


Script:


Gary “It is like giving birth to see it set free is amazing”
Andrew “To see it swim away its rocket it’s just one of best feelings it really is”
Links “Once driven to the verge of extinction, Southern Right Whales have made a dramatic recovery thanks mainly to the protection they are offered in South African waters their natural breeding ground. Unfortunately this also means that more and more of them are becoming entangled in fishing gear. In 2016 alone there were 32 entanglements.
Mike “It is always on a weekend or a Friday or late in the afternoon that’s always the case, it’s always been like that.”
Script: Mike Meyer heads up the South African Whale Disentangling Network, a volunteer group which is part of a global initiative to deal with entanglements
Mike Meyer” In 2005 we had a huge increase in the number of entanglements and we had some well-meaning but quite untrained people going out to sea and jumping in the water with whales and that was a recipe for disaster and a number of people have been killed by whales”
Script: Spearheaded by The Department of Environmental Affairs’, the network was established in 2006 with a core group of 4 people, to date they have trained scores of volunteers
Mike “We have actually made it illegal for members of the public to disentangle a whale. Their idea is to take as much of the entanglement off as possible without fully disentangling the whale and that is committing an animal to a very slow death”
Link “A whale’s natural instinct when encountering fishing gear at sea is to roll over which means they eventually become entangled in the line. 72 % of the whale population have scars from fishing line and 90% of those that become entangled eventually die.”
Script: Steven McCue is right on the front line as the team’s cutter, it’s a highly skilled and physically tough job
Steven “Humpback whales are usually more docile than Southern Right whales Southern right whales are a scary animal to work with because Southern Right whale can swipe his tail sideways and up and down where a Humpback tends to mostly just go up and down with a Southern Right you are not actually sure of where to go
Mike “Everybody’s heart takes a huge drop when it’s a right whale and then the adrenaline really starts to pump
Script: The NSRI’s Andrew Ingram describes his first disentanglement
Andrew “The animal we were disentangling was a Southern Right Whale probably going 18 or 20 meters, it was a very very big animal and at one stage it swam underneath the boat and I remember looking over the side and you can see the eye looking up at you and you just think please don’t flap your tail now
Script: Every disentanglement is used for research which Lieze Swart documents in detail
Lieze “It is so difficult to have a GPS position you take an hour to go out, once you are out at sea that whale could have moved 10-15 miles it could have swum already. So then you have to do these grid searches for hours hours and hours to try and find it.
Mike “There is a huge difference between a whale that is anchored on the bottom and a whale that is free swimming we have got to try and stop that animal and slow it down. We have learnt from the old whalers to use what we call a kegging buoy and we place it on a rope which is attached to the animal and eventually brake it to the stage it will actually stop”
Link “A fully grown adult female Southern Right can weigh up to 50 tons and their tails and flukes pack a massive punch the untangling operations often last for several hours because the whales don’t always co-operate
Upsound Steven getting hit
Steven “I couldn’t actually recall what happened directly after that I know the pole was slapped out of my hand once we recovered the pole the blade was completely snapped off “
Lieze “I don’t know how he does it, sometimes he is hanging over the boat they are holding him by the legs and he is putting his head under the water to get a clearer picture of what’s happening – it’s pretty scary stuff “
Mike “One of our main protocols is that nobody gets into the water. When people get into the water there is a good chance they may get caught by the entanglement and actually dragged under because they think you are actually a predator
Steven “We try and avoid the strong ends of this animal the tail and the flippers but sometimes its unavoidable, sometimes you have to basically get on top of this animal to do the disentanglement”
Script: Gary Nel has been helping free whales for the last 3 years and was the first commercial fishermen to take the disentanglement course. Octopus traps are extremely heavy, and the NSRI boats are often just too small to cope
Gary “The whale must have had well over 500 meters of 5 lobster nets rope attached to him the danger comes if you start cutting the ropes and he starts getting some freedom to move he can dive he can kick a hole in the side of the boat. A 30 ton whale will take this boat down in a flash
Script: Most disentanglement happen in False Bay and Gary’s larger boat is sometimes essential to assist with lifting the tail, but he fears that in the future he won’t get there in time
Gary “With our mooring we are not able to be in Kalk Bay because there is no space for us we are not able to be in Simonstown False Bay yacht club won’t allow us to be in there we are now in Hout bay which is 8 hours away.
Script: Some Whale species can only stay under water for 10 minutes, so drowning is a real possibility, but more likely is the whale will drag the traps and nets taking up to 6 months to die
Lieze “You know the rope will just keep on cutting deeper and deeper and deeper if it is around the mouth then their feeding is impaired if it is around the flippers their swimming is impaired and it can cut so badly into through the skin into the blubber into the flesh and then they get systemic infections and it’s just a long slow death”
Script: Gary added weight to the lines between his octopus traps to deduce entanglements
Gary We have no permit conditions to tell us to put any mitigation factors in place we have done that on our own accord and we splice in sinking, unlike when we first started we used floating rope and we realised the rope was too high off the ground. The design of that gear was taken by our detangling unit to a whale conference last year in Boston.
Andrew “When you are making those first cuts and you are trying to get the rope off it’s like a baby crying, there is a very high pitched distressed sound and the ropes start to fall away the sound changes to a much deeper more content sound and as that last rope falls away very often the animal will dive it will surface 100 meters or so and blows and then it swims away and it really feels like it is saying thank you.”
Script: Recently quite uncharacteristically a humpback whale hung around for 20 minutes after it was freed, resting its head on the boat
UPSOUND
Link “ It’s taken many years to get the fishing industry on board their involvement in tipping off the disentanglement unit is absolutely vital”
Script: Crayfishermen Frank Symes and Malcolm Jacobs say there can be 40 boats out at any one time, turning the sea into a mass of ropes
Frank “There were three in one day that were tangled and the one we helped and managed to get the rope off
Malcolm “We have already saved many whales lives there at Dassen Island. We call the captain and then he calls Mike …and I feel happy in my heart to save a whale’s life
Mike “We all realise we are not actually solving the problem we know it’s an animal welfare issue we do remove what we can but we are working closely with the industry
Andrew “Mike Meyer is a legend, he is absolutely an incredible man who is so passionate, he spends hours and hours and often his own money in helping to train people, and the sea rescue crews they do it because they really care and I think that’s so cool
